summary:
Marswalk is our attempt to make exploring Mars a little more practical. We built an interactive route-planning system for Jezero Crater that combines real NASA terrain data, AI-based hazard estimation, and scientific points of interest to help plan a potential astronaut traverse.

Our system analyzes terrain slope and roughness, identifies areas of scientific interest using mineral data from NASA's CRISM instrument, and uses our custom-trained AI model, HazardNet, to estimate terrain hazards. It then plans a route through five science stops while continuously calculating the time needed to return to the starting point within a limited EVA window.

But we didn't want this to remain just another map. We also developed an interactive web experience and a mixed-reality application for Meta Quest 3, allowing users to explore the Martian terrain at different scales and even step into the planned route.

We believe that future Mars exploration needs more than just a way to get from one place to another. It needs a way to balance safety, scientific discovery, and the realities of exploring an unfamiliar world.
details:
Marswalk brings together several different pieces of technology to tackle one problem: how could astronauts explore an unfamiliar part of Mars while making informed decisions about where to walk and when to return?

We focused on a 1.5 × 1.5 km area of Jezero Crater, using real terrain data from the HiRISE camera on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. We processed elevation and imagery to create a detailed terrain grid containing information about slope and roughness. We also incorporated mineral signals from NASA's CRISM data to identify five scientifically interesting locations, particularly areas with carbonate and olivine signatures.

One of our main components is HazardNet, a custom U-Net-based AI model trained from scratch. It analyzes terrain imagery and estimates whether an area should be classified as go, careful, or avoid. These estimates are incorporated into our route planner, which considers slope, roughness, terrain hazards, and scientific value when calculating a route. We also account for the limited duration of an extravehicular activity (EVA), calculating the time required to walk back at every point along the route. Our current planning model uses a 240-minute EVA limit and a typical-sol daylight window; these are planning assumptions rather than certified mission limits.

We wanted people to experience this environment rather than simply look at numbers on a screen. We therefore developed an interactive web map with 2D and 3D terrain visualization, alongside a mixed-reality application for Meta Quest 3. Users can place a holographic version of the terrain on a surface, step into it, follow the planned route, and explore features such as return routing, hazard indicators, and Perseverance's actual traverse.

Our development involved Python, machine learning with PyTorch, FastAPI, JavaScript, Three.js, WebXR, and Leaflet, alongside NASA's planetary datasets and APIs. We also considered terrain uncertainty, limited exploration time, scientific priorities, visibility, and the limitations of using orbital data to estimate ground-level hazards.

What makes Marswalk exciting to us is the way it connects planetary science, AI, route optimization, and mixed reality into one interactive exploration experience. Rather than treating safety and scientific discovery as separate goals, we wanted to explore how both could be considered when planning a journey on another world.

Results: our demo route covers 4.4 km through five science stops and keeps at least 136 minutes to walk back at every point. HazardNet reaches a mean IoU of 0.369 on held-out terrain, against 0.232 for a majority baseline. On Perseverance's real 6.69 km traverse, our planner's routes stay closer to the rover's path than a straight line (median 16.0 m vs 20.0 m) and cross less steep ground. These checks validate the map against terrain data and rover experience, not astronaut safety; Marswalk is a planning concept, not a certified safety system.

Try it (no login): web map https://phobos-display.vercel.app | Meta Quest 3 or PC https://phantom-phobos.vercel.app | code https://github.com/mahyda07/phobos-phantoms

Use of AI: HazardNet is our own model, trained during the hackathon. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with code, tests and documentation; this is declared in AI_USAGE.md and in file headers. The headset's spoken callouts are synthetic voice clips made with the Windows speech synthesizer and are also shown as on-screen captions. No AI-generated images or video are used, and no NASA branding is used or modified.
